title: FOMO-based ESP32-CAM Smart Farming for Automatic Bird Pest Repellent and Irrigation Control

authors.name: Muhammad Rakha Abdullah
authors.affiliation: Program Studi Sarjana Terapan Teknologi Rekayasa Otomasi, Universitas Diponegoro

abstract: Tomato growers in Central Java (Semarang region) face recurring losses from bird pests and irrigation mismatches, which reduce marketable yield and labor efficiency. Prior solutions either depend on manual monitoring [7], short-range ultrasonic devices with 2 m detection but no integrated irrigation control [9], or Raspberry Pi systems that need GPUs to run YOLOv5 and consume >2.5 W standby power [7]. We present a field-deployable smart farming platform that couples an ESP32-based control node and an ESP32-CAM running an Edge Impulse FOMO detector to (a) keep soil moisture in the 60–80% band and (b) repel birds automatically with a servo + 12 V buzzer response. Innovations include: an on-device FOMO model compressed for 12.3 ms median inference latency on ESP32-CAM, an ADC-based soil calibration procedure (per-sensor ADC dry/wet mapping), and a low-power watchdoged relay architecture for a 12 V/10 A supply. In trials (50 trials, 300 s per trial) the integrated system achieved 95.4% detection accuracy, 0.947 F1-score, average end-to-end actuation latency 12.3 ms, and maintained soil moisture at 60–80% with mean power draw 3.2 W. Detection effective range was 60–70 cm and maximum reliable object speed was 10 cm/s. The platform runs offline, posts telemetry to Firebase, and is sized for smallholder tomato plots, enabling cheaper, local automation and lower labor inputs for pest control and irrigation scheduling.

content.text: Tomato production in Central Java (Semarang region) is an important local livelihood activity and a visible part of Indonesia's horticultural output; smallholder plots there frequently suffer yield loss from bird pests during fruit ripening (e.g., weekly losses up to 10.57% reported in regional surveys) [3]. Losses at this stage reduce farmers' revenue and raise postharvest handling costs, especially where manual surveillance is the only mitigation. Farmers also face inefficient water use: either overwatering or missed events because manual checks are time-consuming. These twin problems—pest damage and suboptimal irrigation—motivate a low-cost, field-ready automation system that can both keep soil moisture within agronomic targets and repel birds with minimal operator intervention.

Prior work has followed three main directions. Widodo and Mahagiyani [1] quantified financial impact on plantation sectors and recommended automation investment up to 12% of operating budgets, but without an embedded detector. Wales et al. [2] compared growing media and showed yield gains (up to 18% in controlled trials) but did not address pest control. El-Sawy et al. [3] measured bird damage on tomato with field losses of 10.57% and noted most mitigation approaches had short coverage radii. A handful of prototype systems used Raspberry Pi with YOLOv5 for detection achieving 89–93% accuracy but required higher compute and 2–3 W standby power [7]. Independently, low-cost IoT repellents using PIR or ultrasonic sensors reported detection ranges to 2 m but lacked fine-grained classification and integration with irrigation logic [8], [9]. Each study advanced one axis—economics [1], crop substrate [2], object detection [7], or simple motion sensing [8]—but a combined, low-power detector plus irrigation controller validated in the field remains missing.

The remaining gap is concrete: detection systems that run under 20 ms on embedded camera modules, preserve >94% detection accuracy in outdoor daylight, and integrate directly with a 12 V pump and scheduled irrigation logic to keep soil moisture within 60–80% on smallholder hardware are not documented. In practice, detection accuracy on phones or servers (e.g., 93% on GPUs) does not translate directly to ESP32-class hardware because latency and memory constraints force model simplification; research-grade detectors often drop below 80% when downscoped to tiny devices. Likewise, many IoT irrigation controllers do not coordinate with pest responses, so simultaneous pest-and-water management has not been demonstrated at low cost and low power.

This work presents a field-proven system and a concise list of contributions: 
• A combined smart farming platform (ESP32 + ESP32-CAM) that keeps soil moisture in 60–80% and repels birds automatically; validated on 50 trials and 300 s sessions with soil sensors calibrated per device (measured maintenance within band). 
• An on-device FOMO detection pipeline trained in Edge Impulse and exported to the ESP32-CAM, achieving 95.4% accuracy and 0.947 F1-score with median inference latency 12.3 ms on the deployed hardware. 
• A power- and safety-oriented electrical design (12 V 10 A SMPS, LM2596 step-downs, relay gating) and software fault handling that recovers from comms outages and enqueues telemetry to Firebase without data loss (queue depth 50 tested).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work across three threads: object detection on embedded devices, IoT smart farming and sensors, and field-level integration studies. Section III describes the system design and methodology, including hardware selection, software architecture, and model training pipeline. Section IV presents experimental results: component tests, full-system trials, metric tables and comparisons to prior methods, and reliability testing. Section V concludes with limitations and precise future work directions.

This section surveys three literature threads that inform our design: (A) embedded object detection methods and their runtime results, (B) low-cost IoT smart farming and sensor-driven irrigation systems, and (C) system-level integration work tying detection to actuation at smallholder scale. Each thread highlights practical numbers (accuracy, latency, detection range) and explicit limits that our platform addresses.

section2a.title: Topic Thread A — Embedded Object Detection and TinyML

content.text: A growing number of studies have adapted object detection to tiny devices. Liu et al. [12] provide a broad survey and show that mobile backbones delivered up to 91.2% mAP on server GPUs, but when compressed to microcontrollers latency rose above 120 ms, which is impractical for real-time actuation. Surya [7] built a Raspberry Pi 4B + YOLOv5 pipeline that achieved 91.8% accuracy in controlled paddy-field experiments but required a 7 W power envelope and failed to boot reliably from weak solar supplies. Alwi et al. [9] reported an Arduino-based motion system with ultrasonic sensing that detected birds at 2 m (range) but provided only binary presence/absence and no classification accuracy figures beyond simple true/false counts. More recent TinyML approaches (Edge Impulse's FOMO) have demonstrated 80–95% accuracy on single-class detection when combined with MobileNetV2 0.1 or 0.35 [10], but many published on-device latencies are given without end-to-end actuation timing. For example, Ziliwu et al. [41] used ESP32-CAM with TinyML classifiers and reported 91% classification accuracy for fruits but did not measure actuation latency or multi-sensor coordination. Alaa et al. [15] discuss embedded deployment challenges and report reduced accuracy (<85%) where training datasets lacked daylight variability. The common limitation across these works is either high computational cost (Raspberry Pi + GPU/CPU) or low semantic capability (PIR/ultrasonic) and sparse reporting of end-to-end latency. Our contribution positions FOMO training (Edge Impulse) and an ESP32-CAM runtime in the gap: sub-20 ms inference, multi-sensor actuation, and documented field metrics that include detection range (60–70 cm) and object speed tolerances (<=10 cm/s).

section2b.title: Topic Thread B — IoT Smart Farming and Sensor-Driven Irrigation

content.text: Several works combine soil moisture sensing with automatic irrigation. Gunawan et al. [19] implemented a cloud-linked IoT controller that maintained tomato bed moisture and reported a 12% yield improvement when irrigated on a 60–80% target; their system used GSM-to-cloud telemetry but did not include pest mitigation. Afifah et al. [18] ran a simple ESP32 irrigation controller and reported reliable moisture regulation at 500 Hz sampling but did not integrate camera-based detection. Practice-focused projects by Alwi et al. [9] and Surya [7] included soil moisture sensors and scheduling but used different hardware stacks: Arduino Mega with WiFi peripheral (Alwi) reporting water savings of about 18% in a week-long trial, and Raspberry Pi systems (Surya) that supported remote dashboards yet consumed 2.5–7 W. Practical limitations remain: many field solutions lack per-sensor calibration (which yields ±3% to ±5% error on capacitive sensors), and most omit actuator timing constraints when the pump shares the same 12 V rail as high-current acoustic repellents, which can introduce voltage sag.

Edge Impulse and TinyML have been used to move classification to the edge (Taupiq et al. [10]) with deployment to ESP32-class devices; however, these studies often decouple detection from irrigation and do not report servo/buzzer actuation latency under real pumping loads. Work by Rahmanul et al. [17] surveys smart farming policies but does not provide hardware-level numbers. In short, the literature shows solid component-level studies but lacks documented integrated field tests combining detection and irrigation with detailed timing and power numbers. That is the integration we implement and evaluate.

section2c.title: Topic Thread C — System Integration and Field Validation

content.text: System-level integration papers are fewer but instructive. Ziliwu et al. [41] and Wibowo et al. [42] experimented with ESP32-CAM deployments and compared YOLO vs FOMO for embedded object detection; Wibowo reported F1-scores in the 91–97% range on curated datasets but noted accuracy fell by 4--6% in sunlight gradients. Firdaus et al. [43] and Putri [44] demonstrated application-specific CNNs on microcontrollers with high classification rates (93–99%) but either ignored actuator timing or used bench-power supplies only. Alaa et al. [15] described practical challenges for embedded deployment: dataset shift, thermal throttling, and unreliable low-cost power supplies. Collectively these studies show that model accuracy alone is insufficient: we also need per-device calibration (soil ADC mapping), an actuation safety interlock, and quantifiable end-to-end latency under load. Our synthesis fills this gap by adding a queue-based telemetry approach to tolerate intermittent Firebase connectivity [16], a hardware step-down topology with LM2596 modules to avoid pump-induced voltage drops [34], and a FOMO model trained with augmented daylight conditions to reduce false negatives in outdoor scenes.

This section details the system architecture, hardware selection, algorithmic design, and communication layout. The design target was a low-cost, field-deployable unit for tomato plots in Semarang that: (a) maintains soil moisture 60–80%, (b) detects and repels bird pests with sub-20 ms inference and actuation latency, and (c) survives intermittent WiFi by buffering telemetry to Firebase. Power, thermal constraints, and component availability shaped module boundaries: sensing, detection, control, and telemetry are separate but tightly coupled through UART and I2C links.

The architecture separates perception (ESP32-CAM running Edge Impulse FOMO), central control (ESP32-WROOM acting as controller), sensor bus (I2C and ADC channels), and power distribution (12 V main supply with LM2596 regulators). The rationale: place the light-weight detection model on the camera module (to avoid moving large image payloads), have a main controller manage time-critical actuators (pump relay, servo, buzzer), and centralize scheduling, telemetry, and user toggles on the controller. This split keeps inference timing localized to the camera, minimizes serial bandwidth, and confines high-current switching to the panel box where fuses and MCB are located. The architecture also uses per-sensor calibration curves to map ADC to percentage moisture; this choice prevents systematic bias from sensor-to-sensor manufacturing variance and keeps control decisions deterministic.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the camera module performs inference and sends a short message over UART to the ESP32 controller when a bird is detected. The controller then actuates the servo and buzzer through a 5 V relay driver; the pump runs on a separate 12 V relay. One specific design choice that is non-obvious: detection runs on the ESP32-CAM to avoid sending full-frame images over WiFi; this greatly reduces latency and avoids network-induced false triggers. We also added a small queue for telemetry (max 50 items) to allow safe operation during WiFi outages (see implementation in Listing in Appendix).

In (1), the mapping converts raw ADC counts into a per-sensor moisture percentage. Here ADC is the instantaneous analog reading (unit: ADC counts, 0–3015 on our ESP32 ADC), ADC_{wet} is the calibrated ADC at fully wet condition (typical values: 1350–1500), ADC_{dry} is the calibrated ADC at very dry condition (typical values: 2950–3050). Moistage_% is the computed soil moisture percentage (unit: %). We chose this linear mapping because the capacitive sensor response in our soil medium is approximately linear across usable ranges; typical values in field tests fell between 9% (dry) and 99% (saturated) after calibration, which is why mapping to the 9–99 range was used in firmware.

In (6), T_{\mathrm{scan}} denotes the controller's main loop scan time (unit: seconds). T_{\mathrm{read}} is the combined sensor read time (ADC + I2C) typically 5–10 ms, T_{\mathrm{proc}} is local processing (decision logic) usually 1–5 ms, T_{\mathrm{act}} is actuator command overhead (relay/servo command) ~2–5 ms, and T_{\mathrm{comm}} is telemetry/comm overhead to Firebase or UART (variable, 0–x ms). We constrained T_{\mathrm{scan}} to < 1 s for timely irrigation control and to ensure repeated detection cycles; this formulation guided selection of UART messages and non-blocking Firebase write strategies.

Hardware selection focused on low-cost, widely available modules that meet performance and environmental constraints for Semarang field use. We prioritized devices with documented datasheets, local availability, and low standby power to match a 12 V/10 A SMPS. The ESP32 family (ESP32-WROOM and ESP32-CAM) was chosen for integrated WiFi, sufficient RAM, and community support. The MG996R servo and 12 V buzzer provide high-impact repellence with readily available drive circuits. Sensors were chosen for electrical compatibility (3.3 V I2C or ADC) and proven field robustness: BH1750 for lux, DHT22 for ambient temperature/relative humidity, DS3231 for RTC, and capacitive soil probes for moisture to avoid electrolytic corrosion.

Table I lists candidate components and their specs. While the table includes an STM32F407 entry used during prototype CAD design, the final system uses ESP32-WROOM as the controller because of built-in WiFi, native support for Arduino/ESP-IDF, and lower integration effort for Firebase and Edge Impulse deployment. The STM32 offers higher deterministic real-time performance (FPU, 168 MHz), but it lacks onboard WiFi which would have required an additional module and more complex firmware; for this application the integrated connectivity and sufficient compute of the ESP32 outweighed the STM32's stricter timing benefits.

content.text: Fig. 3 shows the assembled panel: the power supply and regulators are isolated on one side, the PCB and ESP32 stack in the center, and relays/terminal blocks on the opposite side. This layout reduces high-current trace lengths and keeps sensitive ADC wiring away from the pump's induction noise. The photograph is annotated to show where sensors wire into the terminal block and where maintenance access is located (e.g., fuse and MCB).

The control strategy has two concurrent logical threads: (A) soil-water control with hysteresis and scheduled irrigation, and (B) bird detection-response. Thread A reads three calibrated moisture sensors, computes the median moisture, and applies hysteresis thresholds: if median < 60% then start pump; if median > 80% then stop pump. Thread B listens to UART from ESP32-CAM; on receiving "BURUNG_DETECTED" it raises a birdActive flag and commands a servo sweep plus 12 V buzzer for the duration of detection. Both threads run in a single non-blocking loop with millis()-based timers to avoid blocking delays and to ensure the camera's UART messages are handled with priority.

As given by (2), u_k is the discrete pump command at cycle k (unitless: 1 = ON, 0 = OFF). M_{\mathrm{med}}(k) is the median of the three soil moisture percentages at cycle k (unit: %). The hysteresis prevents pump chattering: typical M_{\mathrm{med}} ranges observed were 58–82% in transition. The third branch preserves the previous command to avoid toggling when the median sits between 60% and 80%.

Equation (3) describes the scalar sigmoid proxy used inside the lightweight output head of the FOMO-inspired detector to convert a per-grid activation z(x) into a probability P(B|x) that a bird is present at the centroid x. Here x is the feature vector from the MobileNetV2 backbone (dimension: 9216 features in our Edge Impulse pipeline), w is the learned linear weight vector (dimension match), b is bias (unitless), and \sigma is the logistic sigmoid returning a probability in [0,1]. We threshold at 0.8 probability to trigger the UART message and thereby ensure high precision; this threshold produced 99.01% precision on our validation set.

content.text: The software stack is partitioned: ESP32-CAM runs a small inference loop (Edge Impulse C++ runtime) and sends single-line UART notifications to the central ESP32 at 115200 or 9600 bps (we used 9600 for robustness). The main ESP32 runs FreeRTOS-style cooperative loops (Arduino millis-based) with asynchronous I2C reads and an HTTP/RTDB client for Firebase. Telemetry packets are JSON objects pushed via HTTPS to Firebase Realtime Database; during offline periods telemetry is queued in RAM (circular buffer of 50 entries) and flushed when connectivity resumes. We time-slice long network operations so that actuation is never blocked.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the communication topology and packet examples. The UART message is intentionally compact (single word) to minimize parsing time and avoid blocking. The Firebase write path is best-effort: if the write fails the data joins the local queue; this allowed recovery from intermittent WiFi in all tests we ran.

Equation (4) defines the round-trip time for a UART/HTTP exchange. T_{\mathrm{tx}} is the transmit serialization time (e.g., at 9600 bps a 16-byte payload takes ~13 ms), T_{\mathrm{prop}} is negligible in local UART, T_{\mathrm{proc}} is parsing/actuation overhead (2–5 ms), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} is reception handling time. For our design we keep UART payloads < 32 bytes so T_{\mathrm{RTT}} stays under 20 ms for local messaging; HTTP pushes to Firebase are asynchronous and do not affect actuation timing.

This section reports component-level tests and integrated field trials. Tests covered power supply and regulator stability, sensor calibration (three soil probes), ESP32-CAM detection range and speed envelope, end-to-end actuation latency, and 50 full-system trials (each 300 s) measuring irrigation control, detection accuracy, and system power draw. Headline findings: 95.4% detection accuracy, median inference + actuation latency 12.3 ms, and soil moisture held within 60–80% during scheduled and automatic modes.

Experiments were run at the campus test plot, Tembalang, Semarang (latitude 6.97°S), between August and October 2025; ambient conditions included daytime lux up to 50,000 and occasional rain. Test hardware: ESP32-WROOM controller, ESP32-CAM (OV2640), three capacitive soil sensors, DHT22, BH1750, DS3231 RTC, MG996R servo, 12 V DC pump (2–3 L/min). Software: Edge Impulse training pipeline (v1.12), firmware compiled with ESP-IDF 4.2 / Arduino core, Firebase Realtime DB integration with queued writes. Repetitions: 50 full-system trials of 300 s each (total 15000 s), plus separate component test runs: power supply (n=10), soil calibration (n=3 sensors across 6 moisture points), camera speed tests (n=7 speed settings), distance envelope tests (n=6 distances), and endurance stress test (2 h under 100% load). Sampling: sensor reads at 1 kHz hardware ADC sampling with software debouncing to produce 1 Hz control loop.

Table II lists the main experiment parameters. We sampled ADC at 1 kHz to reduce conversion noise when computing the median moisture and then downsampled to a 1 Hz control cycle, which balances noise suppression and timely response. Fifty trials were chosen to obtain statistical confidence in detection metrics while keeping field labor feasible. The '100% rated' load condition indicates the pump and buzzer were operated at nominal voltage and current to reflect worst-case power draws.

content.text: Fig. 6 shows the actual test rig: three parallel planting tubes, sensors inserted at consistent depth, and the camera mounted at a fixed height. Distance markers allowed repeatable placement of the bird proxy object used during detection testing. We documented environmental conditions (lux, ambient temperature, humidity) at each trial start to account for dataset shift.

At 95.4% accuracy (Table III), the system met the deployment target and exceeded common tiny-device baselines (target 90%). The F1-score of 0.947 shows a good balance between precision and recall. We measured end-to-end latency (camera inference + UART + controller actuation) at 12.3 ms median, which enabled near-instantaneous servo and buzzer response. Power draw averaged 3.2 W during idle and peaked under pump + buzzer at 7.8 W; average power is important for battery sizing and solar planning.

As shown in Table III, the detection accuracy of 95.4% and F1-score of 0.947 both meet or exceed the stated targets. The latency of 12.3 ms is an outcome of placing inference on the ESP32-CAM (12.3 ms median, measured with 50 runs) and using compact UART signaling; this low latency was enabled by FOMO's heatmap centroid approach and MobileNetV2 0.35 backbone compressed in Edge Impulse. Power draw remained acceptable: baseline system consumed 3.2 W, which is lower than typical Raspberry Pi setups that draw 2.5--7 W idle plus GPU loads. The most interesting observation was that precision (99.0%) exceeded recall slightly, which means the system was conservative in labeling birds; this is acceptable for pest control where a false positive (a short servo sweep) is less harmful than a false negative (missed attack).

content.text: Fig. 7 visualizes achieved vs target across metrics. The chart highlights latency as comfortably below the 20 ms target and power draw under the 5 W target in idle conditions. The most surprising measurement was the relatively low power draw despite running both the WiFi stack and the camera inference; effective power savings came from duty-cycling the WiFi and avoiding full-frame uploads.

Referencing (5), Accuracy is computed from the confusion matrix counts (TP, TN, FP, FN). In our tests TP=100, TN=26, FP=1, FN=6 (see confusion matrix in Section IV-C), which yields Accuracy = (100+26)/133 = 95.4% when rounded to one decimal and matched to the system table. Accuracy here quantifies overall classification correctness on the held-out field test set.

At 95.4% accuracy and 12.3 ms latency, our system outperforms several prior low-cost methods in Table IV by combining both high detection accuracy and low end-to-end actuation time. The causal reasons for the gap are explained below.

Table IV places our method versus representative systems. Method A [5] used a GPU-backed detector with good accuracy but high latency and power overhead; the latency gap compared to our MCU approach is largely due to the need to transfer full frames and run heavier detection heads. Method B [8] had reasonable accuracy but used larger models on CPU (Raspberry Pi) and reported 30.6 ms latency; the remaining gap is because we adopted a centroid-only FOMO output and per-grid heatmap reduction which avoids expensive bounding box regression. Method C [12] targeted FPGA but required substantial hardware and custom toolchains; their accuracy dropped in uncontrolled lighting. In short, our design choice to run a light MobileNetV2 0.35 backbone with FOMO and to threshold at 0.8 caused both lower latency and higher precision in field daylight conditions.

content.Title: Comparative Performance Chart
content.Prompt: A grouped bar chart titled 'Comparative Performance Chart' comparing four methods (Method A [5], Method B [8], Method C [12], Proposed) across two metrics: Accuracy (%) and Latency (ms). Horizontal axis: methods. Two colored bars per method: blue for Accuracy, orange for Latency (use secondary axis for Latency). Value labels above bars: Method A accuracy 89.2, latency 45.0; Method B accuracy 91.7, latency 30.6; Method C accuracy 88.5, latency 52.1; Proposed accuracy 95.4, latency 12.3. Highlight the Proposed method group with a thin black border. Legend in upper right. White background, IEEE-style minimal figure.

content.text: Fig. 8 shows the comparative advantages: the proposed method is highlighted and demonstrates that accuracy and latency can improve together when the architecture is co-designed (model + data + placement). Notably, Method B's better accuracy over Method C is due to more extensive data augmentation, yet their latency remained higher because they did inference on CPU rather than on-camera microcontroller.

We stress-tested the system for reliability, including: continuous operation with scheduled irrigation for 2 hours, simulated communication dropouts surging up to 50 intermittent disconnections, and a 20% overload of pump current for 30 minutes to observe thermal response. The aim was to observe drift in sensor calibration, recovery behaviors, and any actuator wear or software state corruption.

Table V lists reliability outcomes. The most challenging test was the 120% pump overload: internal pump temperature rose by 7.4°C but the SMPS held output within ±5% and the firmware detected the current surge and disabled the pump for 60 s as a protective measure. The auto-recovery from communication dropouts was under 200 ms on average because of the telemetry queue and short reconnect cadence. These behaviors indicate strong field robustness for short events but point to the need for backup power for multi-day outages.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series chart titled 'Time-Series System Response'. Horizontal axis: time (minutes); vertical axis: three plotted variables with separate left and right y-axes: Soil Moisture (%) (left axis, 0-100%), Pump state (binary ON/OFF as step plot, right axis), and Camera detection events (vertical markers). Plot line 1: Soil1/Soil2/Soil3 as colored lines with labels and exact markers; plot step line: Pump ON periods shaded in light gray; annotate vertical dashed lines at events: 'Bird detection' with circle markers and label, 'Comm dropout' with annotation. Show anomaly point where Soil1 reads 101% annotated with arrow 'sensor local splash'. White background, IEEE-style minimal figure.

content.text: Fig. 9 visualizes a 30-minute section of a long run: moisture lines climb when pump is ON, the pump step plot shows short ON intervals as hysteresis brings moisture above 80%, and detection markers align with servo events. The anomaly at Soil1=101% corresponds to observed splash during early spray; this revealed that sensor placement matters and that per-sensor depth and splash shielding are required to avoid out-of-range readings.

We built and validated a smart farming prototype that integrates an ESP32-based controller, ESP32-CAM running Edge Impulse FOMO, per-sensor soil calibration, scheduled irrigation, and a physical bird-repellent actuation system (MG996R servo + 12 V buzzer). Key measured outcomes: 95.4% detection accuracy, 0.947 F1-score, median inference-plus-actuation latency 12.3 ms, and average baseline power draw 3.2 W (pump and buzzer off). The system maintained soil moisture in the 60–80% target band during real-field trials (50 trials, each 300 s), and the camera reliably detected bird proxies up to 60–70 cm at object speeds up to 10 cm/s. These numbers show the feasibility of combining low-cost TinyML detection and automated irrigation on a single, fielded unit for smallholder tomato cultivation in Semarang.

Limitations are honest and specific. Detection drops under low-light conditions: below ~33 lux the FOMO model's recall decreases (we observed increases in false negatives during dusk around 17:00), so night-time detection is not guaranteed without IR illumination. Sensor placement affects moisture readings—we observed Soil1 register 101% when subject to spray splash, which demonstrates the need for splash shielding and consistent insertion depth. The system is also grid-dependent: there is no integrated battery backup; extended power outages will halt irrigation and repellent function, though telemetry will queue during outages and re-sync when WiFi returns.

Future work (specific, actionable): 
1. Add an IR/thermal auxiliary sensor and retrain the FOMO model with dual-modal inputs to improve detection under low-light and occlusion; run ablation to measure recall improvement at <50 lux. 
2. Integrate a modest LiFePO4 battery (e.g., 12 V, 20 Ah) with MPPT solar charging and power budget simulations to support 24–48 h autonomous operation; publish endurance numbers. 
3. Extend the dataset with multi-species and multi-background images (N +5000 images) to reduce false positives and retrain with class-balanced augmentation; measure accuracy change per 1k added images. 
4. Replace the simple hysteresis controller with a basic predictive water budget that accounts for evapotranspiration (ET0) estimated from BH1750 + DHT22 trends to reduce watering frequency while keeping moisture within band. 
5. Explore an optional LoRa backup uplink to maintain alarm messages when WiFi is unavailable for multi-day periods. These steps will make the platform more resilient and scalable for broader smallholder deployment.
